Fitting is one function call. Everything worth learning is in what you do next.

# Fitting {background-color="#0C234B"}

## One call

```python
from scipy import stats

one["years_elapsed"] = (one["date"] - one["date"].min()).dt.days / 365.25
fit = stats.linregress(one["years_elapsed"], one["depth_to_water_ft"])
```

::: {.fragment}
**You cannot regress against a datetime.** Convert to years since the start
first — then the slope comes out in feet per year, which is the number you
actually want to report.
:::

## What comes back

```
slope       2.081 ft/yr
intercept  34.79  ft
r           0.948
r-squared   0.899
p-value     1.6e-189
std error   0.0353 ft/yr
```

::: {.incremental}
- **slope** — the answer
- **r-squared** — the fraction of variance the line absorbs
- **p-value** — probability of a slope this steep if the truth were zero
- **stderr** — uncertainty *on the slope*
:::

::: {.fragment}
Report `2.081 ± 0.035 ft/yr`. A slope without its uncertainty is half an answer.
:::

## On p-values

$10^{-189}$ is not a meaningful number. It is a statement that the question was
never in doubt.

::: {.fragment}
With 379 measurements, almost **any** real trend is "significant".
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
Significance answers *"is it distinguishable from zero?"* It does not answer
*"is it large enough to matter?"* — and the second one is the question water
managers ask.
:::

## Your turn: report it properly

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_report
slope = 2.0814
stderr = 0.0353
r_squared = 0.8993
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_report
summary = f"decline of {slope:.2f} ______ {______:.2f} ft/yr (R2 = {r_squared:.2f})"
print(summary)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_report"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The uncertainty on the slope is the standard error, not the $R^2$. A plus-minus
sign is just a character you can type into the string.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_report"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
summary = f"decline of {slope:.2f} ± {stderr:.2f} ft/yr (R2 = {r_squared:.2f})"
```

`decline of 2.08 ± 0.04 ft/yr (R2 = 0.90)`.

Two decimal places, because the third is not supported by the standard error.
Reporting `2.0814` claims a precision you do not have.
:::
:::

# Residuals {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Where the information is

$$\text{residual} = \text{measured} - \text{predicted}$$

::: {.fragment}
If the model is right, residuals are **patternless noise** around zero.
:::

::: {.fragment}
If they have structure, the model is missing something — and the structure tells
you what.
:::

## The well that looks well-fitted

$R^2 = 0.90$. Mean residual by decade:

```
1930    +1.9
1940    -9.6
1950   -14.6
1960   -12.5
1970    +9.4
1980    -0.9
1990    -7.8
```

::: {.fragment}
Below zero for thirty years, well above it in the 1970s, below again after.
**That is not noise.**
:::

## What the pattern means

::: {.incremental}
- Slow decline while the basin was lightly pumped
- Sharp acceleration through the mid-century agricultural era
- Easing as pumping shifted from irrigation to municipal supply
:::

::: {.fragment}
Three regimes. One straight line averages them and reports a rate describing
none of them.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
**A high $R^2$ with structured residuals means you have fitted the wrong model
well.** Plot the residuals. Every time.
:::

## $R^2$ is not model quality {.smaller}

Fit the same well over 1950–1990 — the period where the line fits best by eye:

| Window | slope | $R^2$ |
|---|---|---|
| full record, 1931–1994 | 2.08 ft/yr | **0.90** |
| 1950–1990 only | 2.36 ft/yr | **0.67** |

::: {.fragment}
$R^2$ went *down* on the better-fitting window.
:::

::: {.fragment}
It is the fraction of **this sample's variance** the line absorbs. The full
record spans a century of decline — enormous variance, easy to explain. A
40-year window has less range, so the same quality of fit accounts for less of it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**You can raise $R^2$ by widening your window.** That should tell you what it is
worth as evidence.
:::

```{pyodide}
    "b": "the model is wrong in a structured way, despite the high R2",
    "c": "there is not enough data to tell",
    "d": "the data are too noisy to fit",
}
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_diag
verdict = ______
print(diagnoses[verdict])
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_diag"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

379 measurements is plenty, and the residuals are large but not random — they
run in decade-long streaks on one side of zero.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_diag"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
verdict = "b"
```

The fix is not more data or a fancier fit. It is **fitting the regimes
separately**, or admitting that a single rate is not the right summary of this
well.

That is a modelling decision, and it comes from the residual plot rather than
from any single number.
:::
:::

# scikit-learn {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Same fit, general interface

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = one[["years_elapsed"]].values   # 2D: (n_samples, n_features)
y = one["depth_to_water_ft"].values # 1D

model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
model.coef_[0], model.intercept_
```

::: {.fragment}
Identical to `linregress` — same least-squares problem. Worth learning because
every other model in the library shares this interface.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**`X` must be 2D**, even with one feature. `df[["col"]]` gives you that;
`df["col"]` does not. `ValueError: Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead` is
the most common scikit-learn error and this is why.
:::

## The split that lies

```python
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25)
```

::: {.fragment}
`train_test_split` **shuffles**. For a time series that scatters the test set
*through* the training period, so predicting it means interpolating between
neighbours you already fitted.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Test MAE on the shuffled split: about **2 ft**. Looks excellent.
:::

## The split that doesn't

Train on 1931–1974, test on 1975–1994:

::: {.incremental}
- train slope: **1.92 ft/yr**
- full-record slope: **2.08 ft/yr**
- test MAE: **15.4 ft**
:::

::: {.fragment}
Seven times worse, on the same data and the same model.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
**A validation scheme that doesn't match how the model will be used will tell
you it works.** For time series, split by time.
:::

## Your turn: pick the split

You want to know whether a trend model can forecast the next decade.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_split
strategies = {
    "a": "train_test_split with test_size=0.25 and shuffle=True",
    "b": "train on everything before a cutoff year, test on everything after",
    "c": "fit on all the data and report the R2",
    "d": "k-fold cross-validation with random folds",
}
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_split
choice = ______
print(strategies[choice])
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_split"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Forecasting means predicting data the model has never seen *and that comes
after* everything it has seen. Which of these reproduces that situation?
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_split"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
choice = "b"
```

Both **a** and **d** shuffle, so the test set is interleaved with training data
and the model is interpolating, not forecasting. **c** doesn't hold anything
back at all.

Only **b** reproduces the actual task. Scikit-learn ships `TimeSeriesSplit` for
the k-fold version of this.
:::
:::
